lines.text: Chapter 1 turned distance into speed. Now go the other way: [[a|from speed to distance]].
lines.say: Chapter one turned distance into speed. Now, let's go the other way.

lines.text: 3 m/s for 4 s is 3 × 4 = 12 m: the [[a|area of this rectangle]].
lines.say: Three metres per second, for four seconds, is twelve metres: the area of this rectangle.

lines.text: But here the speed changes: [[f|$v(t) = t^2$]].
lines.say: But here, the speed changes: v of t is t squared.

lines.text: No single speed to multiply by. So slice up the time.
lines.say: No single speed to multiply by. So slice up the time.

lines.text: In a thin slice, speed barely changes. Treat it as a [[a|rectangle]].
lines.say: In a thin slice, speed barely changes. Treat it as a rectangle.

lines.text: Each is speed × time: the distance covered in that slice. Add them all up.
lines.say: Each one is speed times time: the distance covered in that slice. Add them all up.

lines.text: Thinner slices leave smaller [[f|gaps]] under the curve. The total creeps upward…
lines.say: Thinner slices leave smaller gaps under the curve. The total creeps upward,

lines.text: …and closes in on one number: $\tfrac{8}{3}$, about 2.667 metres.
lines.say: and closes in on one number: eight thirds. About two point six seven metres.

lines.text: Take the limit, infinitely many, infinitely thin slices, and the gaps disappear.
lines.say: Take the limit, infinitely many, infinitely thin slices, and the gaps disappear.

lines.text: Leibniz wrote that limit with a long S, for sum: $\int$. And $\Delta t$ becomes $dt$.
lines.say: Libenits wrote that limit with a long S, for sum. And delta t becomes d t.

lines.text: The integral of speed over time is the distance travelled: [[a|$\tfrac{8}{3}$ m]].
lines.say: The integral of speed over time is the distance travelled: eight thirds of a metre.
The integral adds up infinitely many, infinitely thin slices.
